item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
LUANDA - A cross-border investigation reveals European, British and US oil giants have been routinely spilling oil in Angola’s oceans for 13 years, leaving residents ill and unable to eat. Multiple complaints have been ignored, while fishermen are asked to clean up under ‘voluntary work agreements’.

While Western oil majors pledge a “zero-spill mindset” at home, a year-long investigation - combining on-the-ground reporting from Zaire and Cabinda, exclusive satellite data, and internal documents - reveals a hidden human and environmental crisis along the Angolan coast.

Exclusive satellite analysis of Block 15 (operated by ExxonMobil, and owned by BP, Eni, Equinor and Sonangol) exposes chronic spills covering an area equivalent to at least the size of Montenegro over the past 13 years, vastly contradicting official state figures. On the ground, field interviews show how routine spills poison essential crops, ruin fisheries, and expose residents to carcinogens and toxic hydrogen sulfide gas. Local fishermen reveal they are informally hired to clean up toxic crude with no formal contracts or health insurance, while behind-the-scenes extrajudicial interference stymies legal accountability.

Supported by original field testimony, legal documents, and unpublished satellite imagery, this investigation lays bare the stark double standards and corporate impunity of Big Oil in West Africa.

Key findings

  • Satellite imagery analysis revealed chronic and unreported oil spills around Angola’s Kizomba A field in Block 15 over 13 years. It is operated by ExxonMobil and co-owned by BP, Eni, Equinor and Sonangol.
  • The size of the spill ranges from a minimum cumulative total of 89538 barrels to a possible 4476908 barrels - nearly as much as BP’s Deepwater Horizon disaster. The range occurs because it is not possible to determine the thickness of the oil without physically testing it.
  • The gap between these figures and official records from Angola and the oil giants is stark. Reporting of spills over one barrel is required by Angolan law, but the national oil and gas agency ANPG reports an average of just 450 spilt barrels a year across every offshore block. Similarly, reporting by the oil giants showed very low figures. All of them have state policies of no harm.
  • Wind and current data analysis suggests a portion of the oil may be travelling to the shore. Residents' testimonies support this, noting severe health and agricultural impacts - although they cannot trace the source of the oil to a single block.
  • Residents and health officials report an increase in skin infections, gastrointestinal distress and nausea from the smell of toxic hydrogen sulfide. Health officials shared registries documenting this. Food and fish are blackened by the oil, but many residents are left without any option but to eat them. Cabinda’s ex-health secretary believes there has been a rise in skin cancer because of exposure to the oil.
  • The availability of fish has also drastically decreased, affecting fishermen’s livelihoods as well as available protein sources.
  • Documents show Chevron asked fishermen to clean up a spill under ‘voluntary work agreements’. Workers were given basic rubber boots, gloves and masks, but no formal contracts and no insurance. One ambulance was kept on standby, they reported. They added that this incident was indicative of clean-ups for bigger spills in general across the coast.
  • At least 13 countries worldwide benefit from the oil, including China, India, the United States, Canada, Spain, and Italy. More than 370 million barrels of oil have been shipped to refineries and installations. The chain has links with some controversial entities, such as Trafigura and Glencore as charterers. TotalEnergies, Shell, ConocoPhillips, Sinopec and Sinochem have also acted as charterers, while Sinopec, IOC, Sinochem, Nayara Energy, Repsol and Petronas have bought from the block.

Methodology

This investigation combined open-source and data journalism with on-the-ground reporting.

The team analysed satellite imagery, literature and expert testimony to assess oil spills and their environmental impact. Trade data, ship tracking, corporate records and regulatory research were used to trace the oil, identify companies involved and examine legal and reporting obligations.

Over the course of a year, the team built relationships with Angolan residents and experts before reporting from affected communities along the coast. This included interviews, photo and video documention, access to health records and closed-source legal documents.

The team worked with a whistleblower organisation to ensure informed consent, and protected identities where necessary for safety.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Oil giants’ systematic spills are poisoning Angola’s coast and its communities, Voxeurop, 28/09/2026
  • “Quelle” del blocco 15, il petrolio a perdere che avvelena l’Angola, Domani, 28/09/2026
  • Os derrames sistemáticos das gigantes petrolíferas estão a envenenar a costa de Angola e as suas comunidades, Expresso, 28/09/2026

more to come

COUNTRIES

  • Angola
  • Italy
  • United Kingdom

Team members

Giorgio Michalopoulos

Giorgio Michalopoulos is an Italian journalist based in Brazil.

Stéffie Banatvala

Stéffie Banatvala is a Parsi, British and French freelance investigative journalist.

Mentors

Sam Leon

Sam Leon (London) is a data investigator with experience in both journalism and policy.

Related projects

  • © Ekpali Saint

    The Impact of ENI’s Extractivism in Italy and Nigeria

    IKEBIRI / POTENZA - From the dry hills of southern Italy's Basilicata region to the flood-stricken communities of Nigeria’s Niger Delta, oil giant Eni has left a trail of pollution and environmental degradation spanning continents. This cross-border investigation examines the consequences.

    Meer lezen
  • ©Danil Usmanov

    Kazakhstan: The Cost of Oil

    ATYRAU - As the EU deepens its energy partnership with Kazakhstan, this investigation goes to the source of the oil that helps power European markets. Reporting from Atyrau, Kazakhstan's oil capital, it explores the social and environmental costs of decades of oil extraction.

    Meer lezen

  • The Disappearance of Prespa Lake

    PRESPA LAKE – Prespa lake in North Macedonia is considered even older than the "official" oldest lake in Europe, Ohrid Lake. And it is under threat.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Film / Talks Purple Rain (1984) 27 Sep 2026 / 16:00
item.description:
The film follows The Kid, a talented young man who uses music to escape his abusive situation at home. A member of the band The Revolution, The Kid is the star of the most famous and disputed club in Minneapolis.

When he meets singer Apollonia, The Kid fights not to repeat his father’s abusive patterns, while struggling to keep together his band, threatened by rival musician Morris Day, who wants to take his place.

Part autobiographical, Purple Rain was made to promote the eponymous album, which propelled Prince to the peak of his career: with 25 million copies sold worldwide, it became one of the best-selling albums of all time.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

Biographies

Credits

Director

Albert Magnoli

Genre

Musical

Duration

111 minutes

item.title: Talks Cultivating the murky with ruderal plants 27 Sep 2026 / 16:00
item.description:
As part of the exhibition Inês Zenha. Murky Waters, the artist talks to researcher Teresa Castro about ruderal plants: species that grow and thrive spontaneously in environments disturbed by human activity.

They are not merely the “weeds” of cities and industrial estates, or the successful colonisers of wastelands and urine-soaked tree pits. Flourishing in the everyday ruins of capitalism, they are exceptional companions for thinking and, above all, for cultivating turbulence.

This conversation will be conducted in Portuguese, with simultaneous interpretation into English. The session will also include interpretation in Portuguese Sign Language.

Speakers

Credits

Main image

Inês Zenha, 'Murky-Waters', 2025 (detail of the work) © Sue Ponce, Courtesy Museo CA2M.

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks Summer of Soul (2021) 26 Sep 2026 / 16:00
item.description:
The six-week festival took place at Mount Morris Park (today Marcus Garvey Park), in Harlem, New York City, and featured big names such as Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone, Sly and the Family Stone and B.B. King, amongst others.

Commonly known as the Black Woodstock, the Harlem Cultural Festival drew a crowd of 100 thousand people, although this historic achievement had been erased from the collective memory for almost 50 years.

Registered by Hal Tulchin, the nearly 40-hour footage were archived until they were rescued by the director Ahmir Khalib Thompson. The film was officially launched in 2021 at the Sundance Festival and received several awards, including an Oscar.  

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

Biographies

item.title: Cultural participation across generations: new Evaluation Report now available online
item.description:
The report examines the practices, motivations and barriers to cultural participation among young people, over-65s and people from migrant backgrounds in Piedmont and Liguria, offering insights to inform strategies and initiatives designed to engage diverse audiences.

L'articolo Cultural participation across generations: new Evaluation Report now available online proviene da Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo.

item.title: Concert Tchaikovsky's Serenade for Strings 24 Sep 2026 / 20:00
item.description:
• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

item.title: Conference Conference with the Winner and Jury of the 2026 Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity 24 Sep 2026 / 09:00
item.description:
Bringing together the Prize winner and members of the Jury, the conversation will explore how transformative climate action can generate lasting impact for people and the planet.

Throughout the morning, there will be opportunities to engage with the speakers, take part in a live Q&A and connect with other participants during a dedicated networking session.

The €1 million Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity celebrates outstanding contributions to climate action.

This event will be presented in English with simultaneous translation to Portuguese. It will be livestreamed on this page.

Programme

09:30 – 11:00 / Behind the Winning Initiative: A conversation with the Winner and Jury

11:30 – 12:30 / From Impact to Action: Looking to the Future

The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation reserves the right to collect and keep records of images, sounds and voice for the diffusion and preservation of the memory of its cultural and artistic activity. For further information, please contact us through the Information Request form.

item.title: pigeon rescue and other stuff
Meer lezen
item.description:
GENEVA - The IPCC is one of the most respected scientific institutions in climate research. An investigation into its inner workings now reveals strong links to the Saudi government within its ranks, as well as apparent contradictions of the IPCC’s application of its conflict of interest rules.

The IPCC is the world’s most authoritative international body on climate science. Its reports underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. Yet, its conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing.

This investigation reveals the growing presence of Saudi Arabia, the world's second-largest oil producer, within the IPCC, and present more than 20 cases with significant conflict-of-interest concerns from among the authors selected for their upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Having done background checks for over 200 IPCC authors, the team identified major problems with both the design and application of the organization’s conflict of interest policy, an analysis backed by experts and former IPCC authors.

Key findings

  • At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests. An IPCC vice-chair is also employed by the Saudi energy ministry.
  • The IPCC’s conflict of interest policy is described by experts as failing and this investigation has found discrepancies between what the policy says and the findings on the background checks of about 20 authors of the upcoming 7th Assessment Report.

Methodology

The investigation is based on background checks of 223 authors of the IPCC’s Working Group III for the upcoming 7th Assessment Report. After a thorough search of the authors’ profiles, the team presented its findings to two independent reviewers, as well as to former IPCC authors and experts in several relevant fields. The conflicts of interest were grouped according to their nature and the team has put the list through several rounds of verification until they achieved the final number.

Themes

  • Climate

Publication

ONLINE

  • How Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reports, The Guardian, 21/09/2026
  • Conflits d’intérêts au GIEC : comment l’Arabie saoudite et Aramco ont infiltré le prochain rapport, l'Humanité, 21/09/2026
  • Abbiamo scoperto dei conflitti d’interesse dentro all’IPCC. C’entra il petrolio saudita, Lucy Sui Mondi, 21/09/2026
  • Cómo expertos de la gran petrolera saudí se colaron como autores de los informes climáticos más importantes del mundo, El diario, 21/09/2026

VIDEO

  • Wie unabhängig berichtet der Weltklimarat?, 3Sat, 21/09/2026

FOLLOW-UP

  • Ölexperten aus Saudiarabien arbeiten an zentralem UNO-Klimabericht mit, Tages-Anzeiger, 21/09/2026

COUNTRIES

  • Switzerland
  • Saudi Arabia

Team members

David Haas

David Haas is a freelance investigative journalist and documentary filmmaker from Germany.

Eoghan Gilmartin

Eoghan Gilmartin is an Irish journalist based in Madrid, Spain.

Rita Cruz

Rita Cruz is a Portuguese investigative journalist based in Sweden. 

Silvia Lazzaris

Silvia is an Italian reporter specialising in science and technology. 

Simon Guichard

Simon Guichard is a French investigative journalist based in Paris.

Related projects

  • © Marco Seifert / Der Spiegel

    CCS: The New Promise To Stop Climate Change

    BRUSSELS - The investigation of Annika Joeres and Susanne Götze illuminates a neglected subject of climate policy. They show what a powerful player the Lobby for Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) has become for the European Climate Policy.

    Meer lezen
  • © The Manifold

    Coal and Climate: Examining Greece & Poland

    PTOLEMAIDA - In Greece, coal is considered "national fuel" and policymakers have always treated it as such. The future of the coal industry, however, is not taken for granted. The price of coal has increased, the industry is operating against EU's environmental and economic policies and its proponents and opponents are more than ever at odds. 

    Meer lezen
  • ©Sergio Matalucci

    Melting Societies

    GARMISCH-PARTENKIRCHEN - The Zugspitze, Germany's highest mountain, is home to three of the five glaciers within the country. At least it was.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Conference Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity 2026 Award Ceremony 23 Sep 2026 / 18:30
item.description:
Event Slider

Date

  • 18:30 / Cancelled 18:30 / Sold out Wednesday, 18:30

Location

Pricing

Find out this year’s winner and their contribution to transformative climate action for people and the planet.

Angela Merkel, President of the Jury, will announce this year’s winner at a ceremony bringing together António Feijó, President of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation, and representatives of the winning initiative.

Join us to find out and hear from the winner of the €1 million Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity that celebrates outstanding contributions to climate action.

This event will be presented in Portuguese, Spanish and English with simultaneous translation and with interpretation in Portuguese Sign Language. It will be livestreamed on this page.

Programme

18:45 / Welcome remarks

18:55 / Impact video about the Prize

19:00 / President of the Jury speech and winner announcement

19:10 / Winner Video and Winner Acceptance Speech

19:20 / Concert

19:45 / Closing

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
PUERTOLLANO/VENICE/NAPAJEDLA/MUNICH -Sold as a green industrial revolution, Europe's hydrogen valleys are increasingly a story about lobbying, import dependency and who controls the pipes.

Europe's hydrogen strategy was pitched as a local industrial revival: clean fuel, made and used close to home, replacing fossil imports with homegrown green molecules. Four years on, that vision has quietly shifted into something more geopolitical. Governments and incumbents are re-routing the narrative towards imports, pipeline repurposing and long-distance corridors, while the companies best placed to benefit are the same gas and energy majors that dominated the fossil era, repositioned as the indispensable infrastructure operators of the "green" one.

In Germany, regulatory uncertainty is prompting even funded projects to walk away from public money, while industry consolidates around new lobbying blocs pressing collectively for more state backing, a sign that the sector's centre of gravity is shifting from many small players to a handful of large ones. In Spain and the Czech Republic, the gap between political ambition and delivered infrastructure is exposed by cancelled projects and contested job claims, revealing how easily industrial promises outpace reality on the ground, and how local communities are left to weigh the costs - land, water, disrupted ecosystems - against benefits that often fail to materialise. In Italy, national policy has pivoted from local production to positioning the country as a transit hub between North Africa and Central Europe, keeping legacy gas infrastructure, and its operators, relevant for another generation rather than displacing them.

Across all four countries, the same pattern recurs: hydrogen infrastructure is increasingly shaped to serve strategic and political interests rather than proven industrial demand, with incumbents using the transition to entrench, not disrupt, their position - and public subsidy acting less as a bridge to a new market than as a lifeline for the old one.

Key findings

  • European hydrogen policy is drifting from local, demand-led production towards geopolitical positioning - securing import routes and transit status over genuine domestic capacity.
  • In Germany, funded projects are being abandoned over regulatory uncertainty even as incumbents form new lobbying alliances for further state support.
  • National ambition is being quietly scaled back in several countries, with targets loosened well behind original goals.
  • Flagship projects in Spain and the Czech Republic have met local resistance or outright failure, undercutting the narrative of a smooth, job-creating transition.
  • In Italy, strategy has shifted from local valleys to positioning the country as an indispensable transit corridor, keeping existing gas infrastructure central to the "green" transition.
  • Incumbent players repeatedly occupy dual roles as both lobbyists and beneficiaries of the funding rules they help shape - a structural conflict of interest across several countries examined.

Methodology

Findings combine desk research into EU and national funding frameworks and project registries with original interviews across the four countries - company spokespeople, industry associations, local officials and environmental groups. Claims about project status were cross-checked against multiple independent sources where possible, including site-level reporting and official documentation.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Idrogeno verde, la grande illusione europea, La Via Libera, 15/09/2026
  • Puertollano busca en el hidrógeno su próxima transición industrial, Climatica, 16/09/2026

More to come

COUNTRIES

  • Czech Republic
  • Germany
  • Italy
  • Spain

Team members

Marta Abbà

Marta Abbà is an investigative journalists based in Milan.

Fermín Grodira

Fermín Grodira is an investigative journalists based in Spain.

Mayya Chernobylskaya

Mayya Chernobylskaya is a freelance journalist based in Germany.

Martin Vrba

Martin Vrba is an independent Czech journalist and essayist.

Laura Fazzini

Laura Fazzini is a freelance journalist based in Milan, Italy.

Related projects

  • © Marcos Garcia Rey

    The Chlorpyrifos Case

    BRUSSELS - Residues of Chlorpyrifos, a dangerous insecticide, have been found in fruit baskets and samples of human urine across Europe. This large, cross-border investigation unveils its risks for the public. 

    Meer lezen
  • © Olivia Acland

    Manganese: Green for Europe, Toxic for Georgia

    CHIATURA –  Georgia is a key supplier of manganese, an essential raw material for Europe’s transition to renewable energy which is used in wind turbines and electric cars. This investigation  shows how the EU's rush to secure critical raw materials for its green transition is colliding with weak environmental oversight, opaque corporate networks, and a dramatically shrinking civic space in Georgia.

    Meer lezen
  • © Francesco Pistilli

    Geothermal Divide: Green Ambitions Meet Local Realities

    BIHOR/RADICOFANI - Produced by tapping into the heat stored beneath the Earth’s surface, geothermal energy is regarded as one of the most promising renewable sources, with a largely untapped potential. This investigation explores the different experiences local communities across Europe have with this energy source. 

    Meer lezen

  • Incumbent players repeatedly occupy dual roles as both lobbyists and beneficiaries of the funding rules they help shape - a structural conflict of interest across several countries examined.

Methodology

Findings combine desk research into EU and national funding frameworks and project registries with original interviews across the four countries - company spokespeople, industry associations, local officials and environmental groups. Claims about project status were cross-checked against multiple independent sources where possible, including site-level reporting and official documentation.

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BUCHAREST / SARAJEVO - Mega hydropower projects conceived decades ago during the communist era are now being resumed and developed, ignoring current priorities for water, biodiversity protection, and public spending.

Dams of the Past, Costs of the Present is a cross-border investigation into large hydropower projects in Romania and Bosnia & Herzegovina. First conceived during the communist era (before 1990) they were resumed in recent years, without taking into account technological developments, climate change and in areas that have meanwhile acquired a biodiversity protection regime, with different economic, social and environmental challenges. Despite criticism from experts and opposition from local communities and environmental activists, the projects are moving forward due to the financial interests and political connections behind them.

In Bosnia & Herzegovina, the investigation focuses on the Upper Horizons hydropower scheme, which diverts water through the complex karst system of eastern Herzegovina for electricity production, potentially affecting the Neretva basin and its tributaries to the Adriatic Sea.

In Romania, the projects on the Jiu (Bumbești-Livezeni), Bâsca Mare (Surduc-Siriu) and Răstolița rivers were investigated in particular, because they affect several national parks and Natura 2000 sites, as well as the communities that depend on them.

Together, the cases and stories ask a central question: why are these projects being resumed now, especially given their outstanding financial cost and environmental damage, compared to existing alternatives (wind, solar and battery storage)?

Key findings

  • The Upper Horizons system (Bosnia & Herzegovina) will permanently redistribute water through one of the most complex karst areas in Europe, with potential consequences for the Buna, Bunica and Bregava rivers and the wider Neretva basin. Scientists and environmental groups warn that reduced freshwater flows could increase pressure on ecosystems, endemic species, agriculture and downstream communities, including the Neretva delta in Croatia.
  • The Bumbești-Livezeni project (Romania) involves the capture and dewatering of approximately 30 kilometres of the Jiu River, which is a defining and essential part of the Jiu Gorge National Park. The Răstolița project (Romania) affects the Călimani National Park, a Natura 2000 site, and other protected areas downstream on the Mureș River. The Bâsca Mare dam (Romania), also a piped diversion project (like the Jiu dam), risks leaving a community with several thousand inhabitants who depend on it without water (drinking water, agriculture, livestock farming, tourism).
  • Romania’s energy crisis during summer 2026, was caused by historical minimum flows of the Danube and inland rivers. This confirmed the warnings expressed by specialists, according to which the projects in question will be useless (due to the lack of water) and will not ensure even the expected marginal contribution (less than 1%) to the national energy system. The remaining amounts spent (approximately 450 million euros, only in the case of the three projects investigated) would be sufficient for the installation of solar panels and storage batteries with an installed capacity several times higher.
  • However, in Bosnia & Herzegovina as well as Romania, the development of the projects are moving forward despite disputes over their environmental impact and calls for a reassessment based on contemporary scientific knowledge and climate conditions.
  • Hundreds of millions of euros are involved in the construction and financing of these projects, while questions remain about transparency, public oversight and the long-term financial risks borne by public institutions and companies with majority state capital.
  • The investigation reveals a fundamental conflict between policymakers who present hydropower projects as strategic energy infrastructure and scientists, environmental organizations and affected communities who argue that the half-baked projects need to be reassessed both economically and socially, and above all, before their environmental consequences become irreversible.

Methodology

The investigation combines field reporting, interviews, requests for information and public positions, participation in parliamentary debates, analysis of documents and open source information (OSINT), and cross-border collaboration between journalists from Romania and Bosnia & Herzegovina. Reporters visited the areas affected by the hydropower projects and interviewed local residents, scientists, representatives of civic organizations (local and/or environmental), government representatives, lawyers, public officials, and experts in water engineering, biodiversity, energy and public finance.

Findings from the two countries were compared to identify common patterns in the implementation of hydropower projects conceived decades ago, under fundamentally different environmental, political, and economic conditions.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Gornji horizonti: Projekat iz prošlog vijeka mijenja budućnost Neretve, detektor.ba, 19/09/2026
  • Gornji horizonti: Projekat iz prošlog vijeka mijenja budućnost Neretve, guerila info, 20/09/2026

More to come

FOLLOW UP

Team members

Vladimir Kovačević

Vladimir Kovačević is a long-time journalist from Banja Luka.

Mihai Goțiu

Mihai Goțiu is an investigative journalist with almost 30 years of experience in the local and national press in Romania.

Related projects

  • Small Hydropower Plants Causing Big Damage to Rivers in BiH

    SARAJEVO - This investigation explores the damages caused to nature and small rural communities by the construction of the small hydropower plants and their access roads, and what drove investors, especially foreign ones, to seek opportunities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Meer lezen
  • © Matjaž Tančič

    The Costs of 'Green' Hydropower and Poor River Management

    OSIJEK – Mura-Drava-Danube is a UNESCO-protected biosphere reserve. It spans over 300,000 ha and includes more than 700 km of connected rivers. This investigation reveals poor management practices, lack of cooperation between five national governments, and lack of conservation efforts.

    Meer lezen
  • © Cosmin Filisan

    Climate Change and Mismanagement Deplete Water Reserves in Europe

    BARUTH / ORTONA / TÂRGU NEAMȚ - Across Europe, communities are facing a water crisis fueled by decades of poor groundwater management and climate change. This investigation examines the causes and consequences of water scarcity related to groundwater reserves in three of the most affected EU countries: Italy, Germany, and Romania.

    Meer lezen

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks The Last Waltz (1978) 20 Sep 2026 / 17:00
item.description:
Advertised as a farewell concert, the show attracted an audience of 5000 people and brought together several special guests, such as Bob Dylan (who refused to be filmed until the last minute,  ser filmado até ao último minuto, putting the project’s funding at risk), Eric Clapton, Neil Diamond, Emmylou Harris, Joni Mitchell, Van Morrison and Neil Young, among others.

The concert was filmed by director Martin Scorsese, who transformed it in a 116 minute documentary, considered one of the best film-concerts of all time.

The film includes live performances, interrupted by studio sessions and interviews with musicians Rick Danko, Levon Helm, Garth Hudson, Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson, who reflect on the history of the band and life on tour. 

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Film / Film-Concert / Talks Stop Making Sense (1984) 20 Sep 2026 / 20:00
item.description:
Jonathan Demme follows the band at the height of their career, creating an immersive experience for the audience. The film starts with singer David Byrne alone on the stage, which takes shape gradually as the other elements are brought together.

Filmed during the course of three nights, the documentary includes the band’s first hits, like Psycho Killer, the latest singles at the time, as well as songs from the singer’s solo repertoire and from the Tom Tom Club project, by drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth.  

Hailed by critics as one of the best concert films ever made, Stop Making Sense is an essential film for Talking Heads fans, offering a glimpse into the New Wave scene of the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Film / Talks A Hard Day’s Night (1964) 19 Sep 2026 / 17:00
item.description:
The first Beatles feature film follows the four members of the mythical band, who are preparing for a televised concert, while dealing with a strict manager, hysterical fans ans problematic relatives.

The musicians portray over-the-top comical versions of themselves, recording a period that forever changed the history of music. The soundtrack is taken from the eponymous album, A Hard Day’s Night, edited in 1964.

Filmed during Bob Dylan’s famous transitional period to rock and the electrical guitar, this documentary follows the musician from his arrival in England, on April 26th 1965, and the last concert of the tour at the Royal Albert Hall, on May 10th.

The director had access to the backstage, offering a glimpse into Dylan’s public and private life, from concerts to hotel room conversations, recording his tumultuous relationship with singer-songwriter Joan Baez during a critical phase of his musical career.

A number of well-known figures are featured in the film: Dylan’s agents Albert Grossman and Bob Neuwirth, musicians Donovan, Joan Baez, Marianne Faithfull and Alan Price (Animals), and the beat poet, Dylan’s close friend, Allan Ginsberg, among others.

Don’t Look Back

This event is part of the film cycle “Don’t Look Back”, which includes six documentaries and film-concerts.

item.title: Concert / Talks Sammy Baloji. Missa Utica 19 Sep 2026 / 20:00
item.description:

Missa Utica by Sammy Baloji is a performance that revisits the early contacts between Europe and the Kingdom of Kongo, intertwining colonial memory, spirituality, and music.

In partnership with Contemporânea, the CAM presents, at the intersection of live performance, concert, and artistic montage, Missa Utica (2024) by Sammy Baloji (DR Congo, 1978). The work brings together performers Fiston Mwanza Mujila, Pytshens Kambilo, and Barbara Drazkow Drążkowska in a dialogue with the historical ties between Europe and the Kingdom of Kongo. Memories of colonisation interweave with spirituality, colonial memory, music, and performance.

Based on extensive research conducted by Sammy Baloji on Congolese objects scattered across European collections, Missa Utica returns to the initial contact between Western Christianity and the Central African region, which occurred around the final years of the 15th century. Episodes linked to the evangelical religious conversion of the Kingdom of Kongo, colonial power dynamics, and the resulting cultural and political transformations are revisited within this context.

The title refers to Utica, an ancient Roman city located within the borders of modern-day Tunisia—a place chosen as a symbol, as it was there that the first African bishop of Black descent, Dom Henrique, son of King Afonso I of Kongo, was consecrated. This historical moment serves as a starting point to reflect on how European Christianity spread across the African continent and the relationships it forged with slavery, colonisation, and processes of cultural erasure.

A key highlight of the work is the Missa Luba, a liturgical composition created in the Belgian Congo in the 1950s by Franciscan missionaries, based on traditional Congolese musical styles. Although it gained visibility in Europe and the United States, little was said about the colonial conditions that allowed for its emergence. In Missa Utica, this past resurfaces, but now intertwined with Congolese rumba, recited verses, and improvised sounds.

Throughout the performance, music, text, and image merge into layers; different temporalities occupy the same space without hierarchy. Bodies speak for themselves, bringing forward histories of displacement, resistance, and survival. Voices emerge as traces of struggle and persistence against erasure. In this way, memory does not remain solely in the past—it reappears.

Rather than committing to a single format, Missa Utica blends elements of modern ritual with traces of sound performance. The work follows Sammy Baloji’s ongoing investigation into how colonial archives shape identities, historical narratives, and collective imaginaries.

Missa Utica is part of the Performance Program My Center is Not in the Solar System, under the artistic direction of Celina Brás and curated by Alexandra Balona.

This historical moment serves as a starting point to reflect on how European Christianity spread across the African continent and the relationships it forged with slavery, colonisation, and processes of cultural erasure.

A key highlight of the work is the Missa Luba, a liturgical composition created in the Belgian Congo in the 1950s by Franciscan missionaries, based on traditional Congolese musical styles. Although it gained visibility in Europe and the United States, little was said about the colonial conditions that allowed for its emergence. In Missa Utica, this past resurfaces, but now intertwined with Congolese rumba, recited verses, and improvised sounds.

Throughout the performance, music, text, and image merge into layers; different temporalities occupy the same space without hierarchy. Bodies speak for themselves, bringing forward histories of displacement, resistance, and survival. Voices emerge as traces of struggle and persistence against erasure. In this way, memory does not remain solely in the past—it reappears.

Rather than committing to a single format, Missa Utica blends elements of modern ritual with traces of sound performance. The work follows Sammy Baloji’s ongoing investigation into how colonial archives shape identities, historical narratives, and collective imaginaries.

Missa Utica is part of the Performance Program My Center is Not in the Solar System, under the artistic direction of Celina Brás and curated by Alexandra Balona.

item.title: Talks Murky Waters 19 Sep 2026 / 18:30
item.description:
Inês Zenha talks to curators João Mourão and Luís Silva about the questions running through Murky Waters: the relationship between body, water and transformation, and the ways artistic practice can imagine spaces of resistance, vulnerability and care.

Starting from the paintings, sculptures and installations on display, the conversation turns to the research and production processes behind them, and to themes such as queer embodiment, the materiality of ceramics and painting, and the tensions between the sacred and the profane, purity and contamination.

More than a reading of the exhibition, this is a reflection on how art can create new images, narratives and experiences for thinking about the body and the structures that shape it.

This conversation will be conducted in Portuguese, with simultaneous interpretation into English. The session will also include interpretation in Portuguese Sign Language.

Speakers

Credits

item.title: Talks A Dreamed Conversation 19 Sep 2026 / 17:00
item.description:
During this conversation, Mathieu Copeland, curator of The Exhibition of a Dream, and FM Einheit, who composed and performed the songs based on the dreams of sixteen artists, will revisit the exhibition’s second incarnation since its premiere in Paris in 2017 and reflect on FM Einheit’s artistic trajectory and body of work.

Conceived as a record, The Exhibition of a Dream comprises sixteen dreams interpreted as songs, performed within otherwise empty galleries and following the temporary, evolving forms of mandalas. Drawing direct inspiration from the dreams of filmmakers, playwrights, poets and writers, these sonic compositions unfold over time, tracing patterns that are both fleeting and deliberately constructed.

FM Einheit was invited to take hold of this body of dreams and set it to music. Following initial demos sketched in his Steinschlag studio in Bavaria, FM Einheit collaborated with musicians Volker Kamp, Robert Poss, Susan Stenger, Erika Stucky, Saskia von Klitzing, and the singers of the Gulbenkian Choir. The dream interpretations were recorded live in 2017, both publicly and privately, in the Gulbenkian Foundation’s two amphitheatres in Lisbon: the Open-Air Amphitheatre and the Grand Auditorium. Underscoring the complex beauty inherent in the genesis of a dream, an experience shared within our inner worlds, the exhibition explores what it means to create mental images in the minds of those experiencing these dreams, opening them to new interpretations.

This conversation will be conducted in English, with simultaneous interpretation into Brazilian Portuguese. The session will also include interpretation in Portuguese Sign Language.

Speakers

Covid 19 Bereaved Families for Justice, a Power and Accountability grant holder
Rainbow Project, a Northern Ireland programme grant holder
Cooperation Town, a Sustainable Future programme grant holder
Grants Gulbenkian Energy Communities Supporting renewable energy community projects in Portugal that empower citizens to play an active role in the energy transition. closes 16 Sep 2026 Open call
item.description:
Since Portugal introduced its first legal framework for collective self-consumption of renewable energy in 2019, community-led renewable energy initiatives driven by citizens, associations and local authorities have gradually begun to emerge.

Although Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) offer significant environmental, economic and social benefits, fewer than ten are currently operating in Portugal. RECs enable citizens to come together to generate, share, consume and store renewable energy, creating value both for their members and for the communities in which they operate.

In response to the absence of dedicated public funding for citizen-led Renewable Energy Communities, the Gulbenkian Foundation has partnered with Coopérnico – Sustainable Development Cooperative to support civil society organisations working alongside citizens, local authorities and other local stakeholders.

The initiative seeks to address some of the key barriers to establishing Renewable Energy Communities, including the upfront investment required to launch projects, limited technical capacity within local organisations and communities, and low levels of energy literacy among citizens.

Through this call, the Gulbenkian Foundation expects to fund 10 projects, with grants of up to €30,000 each.

Objectives

Grant funding will be awarded to projects that contribute to:

  • expanding decentralised renewable energy generation and local energy use;
  • strengthening the involvement of local authorities, community organisations and cooperatives in community energy initiatives;
  • promoting collective action through participatory governance models;
  • increasing the participation of economically vulnerable citizens and households;
  • encouraging Renewable Energy Communities in rural and low-density areas, while promoting greater territorial diversity;
  • fostering diversity and representation in project leadership and coordination.

Application process

The call for proposals will take place in two stages.

  • In the first stage, between 14 July and 16 September 2026, applicants are invited to submit an Expression of Interest outlining their proposal to establish a Renewable Energy Community, assessed on the basis of the proposed project and the profile of the lead organisation. The 20 highest-ranked applications will progress to the second stage.
  • In the second stage, between 19 and 30 October, the organisations behind the 20 shortlisted proposals will take part in a two-week online capacity-building programme. Following this programme, and based on the development of the proposals, 10 finalist projects will be selected to receive grant funding from the Gulbenkian Foundation.

Webinar

A webinar to present the call and answer questions will take place on 21 July, from 17:30 to 18:30, with prior registration required, including an open Q&A session.

Conditions

  • Grants are available only to legal entities established and registered in Portugal.
  • The amount awarded to each project will be determined during the final selection process and will not exceed €30,000.
  • Eligible costs include: administrative expenses associated with establishing a Renewable Energy Community; licensing procedures; the purchase and installation of renewable energy generation equipment for collective self-consumption and local energy sharing.

Eligibility

Applications are open to locally based, non-profit legal entities registered in Portugal.

This call is intended to support Renewable Energy Communities at an early stage of development. Therefore, at the time of application, organisations must not have a licensing application pending or already approved by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology in Portugal; or have received funding from any public or private organisation for projects relating to Renewable Energy Communities or collective self-consumption.

How to Apply

  • Only applications submitted online will be accepted;
  • Register at  MyGulbenkian;
  • Before submitting your application form, check all the eligibility criteria and be sure to read the Call Conditions (available in the documents section);
  • Applications may only be submitted once all the mandatory fields of the form have been completed and the documents required under the Call Conditions have been uploaded;
  • Don’t forget to click “submit application”. Try not to submit your application in the last few days leading up to the deadline to avoid any unforeseen last minute problems.

Faq

Who can apply?

This call is open to civil society organisations that represent citizens' interests, are actively engaged with their local communities, and are committed to playing an active role in the energy transition through democratic participation.

Do members of a Renewable Energy Community need to be located within the same parish or municipality?

No. Under Portuguese legislation, members do not need to be located within the same parish or municipality. However, they must be located within 2 km of the renewable energy generation system (or 4 km in low-density areas), or be connected to the same electricity substation.

Can an informal group of citizens apply?

No. The Gulbenkian Foundation provides grants only to legally established non-profit organisations. An informal group of citizens may partner with an eligible organisation whose statutory objectives are aligned with this call, but it cannot receive funding directly from the Foundation.

Can a municipality or parish council apply? What about a local energy agency or another municipal body?

No. This call is intended to support citizen-led Renewable Energy Communities (RECs), meaning communities led by organisations representing groups of citizens, such as associations or cooperatives.

Municipalities, Parish Councils, local energy agencies and other municipal bodies may participate as project partners, but they cannot lead, manage or submit an application.

Is a recently established association, cooperative, foundation or other non-profit organisation eligible?

Yes.

Can an organisation submit more than one application?

No. Each organisation may submit only one application.

Are partnerships required?

No. However, partnerships formally confirmed through Letters of Support submitted with the application may strengthen the quality and feasibility of the proposal.

Are project partners required to make a financial contribution?

No. Partners may contribute in other ways, for example by making rooftops or other suitable spaces available for the installation of photovoltaic panels.

Can a research centre established as a non-profit private legal entity apply?

No. This call is not intended to fund research projects.

Can projects involve partnerships with for-profit organisations?

Yes. Projects may include local businesses or service providers with a relevant role in the community, provided that their participation falls within the scope of their corporate social responsibility activities rather than constituting a commercial service.

These organisations cannot become the sole owners of the project assets. Ownership must be shared.

Will certain territories be given priority?

Yes. Preference will be given to applications from low-density areas or territories facing greater social, economic or environmental vulnerabilities. Applicants should explain and justify these circumstances in their proposal.

Can an organisation that is already receiving funding from the Gulbenkian Foundation apply?

Yes. However, priority will be given to organisations that have never received, or are not currently receiving, funding from the Foundation. Projects that are already being funded by another public or private organisation will not be eligible for support.

Can the grant be used to recruit staff?

No.

What are the requirements for successful applicants?

In addition to managing the grant in accordance with the Foundation's funding rules, successful applicants must participate in all activities organised as part of this initiative, including the capacity-building programme delivered by Coopérnico.

They will also be required to submit a progress report after the start of the project and a final report, using templates provided by the Foundation.

Will there be an information session?

Yes. A free online webinar will take place on 21 July 2026, from 17:30 to 18:30 (Lisbon time). 

Can a national or regional organisation submit a project with a local focus?

Yes, provided that the proposal clearly demonstrates its local relevance.

Can project partners be changed after the application has been approved?

Yes, provided that the change does not compromise the objectives or successful implementation of the project.

Do the future members of the Renewable Energy Community need to be identified in the application?

Applicants should identify the prospective members of the Renewable Energy Community.

Can an organisation with no previous experience in the energy sector apply?

Yes. This call is intended for organisations that consume electricity, not for organisations already operating in the energy sector.

Should the project be selected, the organisation will need to amend its statutes in order to establish a Renewable Energy Community. The costs associated with this process are eligible for funding under the grant.

Can organisations based in the Autonomous Regions of the Azores and Madeira apply?

Yes. Organisations based in the Autonomous Regions are fully eligible to apply.

The only difference concerns the competent licensing authority. In mainland Portugal, the registration, prior control and licensing of Renewable Energy Communities are carried out by the Directorate-General for Energy and Geology (DGEG). In the Autonomous Regions, these responsibilities lie with the Regional Directorate for Energy (DRE) in the Azores and the Regional Directorate for Energy and Climate Change (or Regional Directorate for Energy) in Madeira.

What is meant by "vulnerable citizens or households" for the purposes of this call?

For the purposes of this call, vulnerable citizens or households are those experiencing financial hardship and at risk of energy poverty, as demonstrated by their eligibility for, or receipt of, the Social Electricity Tariff or the Social Natural Gas Tariff.

The aim is to support households for whom energy costs represent a significant financial burden and who stand to benefit most from the cost savings associated with participation in a Renewable Energy Community.

Does an REC have to be based on photovoltaic solar energy?

No. A Renewable Energy Community (REC) may choose other renewable energy generation systems. However, within the scope of this call, only solar photovoltaic generation systems will be considered, as they are currently the most cost-effective technology and the quickest to license and install.

Can a condominium (residential building or multi-family building) apply?

No. A condominium is not eligible because it does not constitute a formally established civil society organization.

Contacts

Questions about this call should be sent to: [email protected].

Before contacting us, please read the Call Conditions carefully and consult the Frequently Asked Questions, as your query may already be answered there.

item.title: What it takes to connect capital and community, with Ralphine Caldwell Charlotte 4 min read
item.description:
• Nelson Hernandez

Overview

Ralphine Caldwell is the senior executive director for LISC Charlotte. The Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC)— one of the largest community development financial institutions in the country — is built on a simple but powerful idea: communities need a real bridge between hard-to-reach capital and the people who need it most.

LISC Charlotte opened in March 2019 to oversee the Charlotte Housing Opportunity Investment Fund. Like its national counterpart, the office pulls investment from the public, private and philanthropic sectors and puts it to work in housing, health, safety, small business support, commercial development, lending and the capacity building of grassroots organizations on the ground.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

When LISC Charlotte looks at bringing an initiative into the city, the first thing that we do is talk to the community. One of the first things that we did was hold community meetings [across] different forums so that we could be clear on the direction community members wanted their neighborhood to take. We’ve been able to uplift projects that have been quite successful in Charlotte, simply because we were able to establish trust early on and the partners know that we have their best interests at heart.

What tools, skills or supports do you rely on to make this work happen?

None of the work or the success of LISC Charlotte would ever have happened without the LISC Charlotte team. I have an amazing staff; all of them have been with the organization since day one. They’ve been on the team for seven years and none of the work that we do [investing over $173 million in Charlotte since the office opened] would be possible without them.

What would you say is the toughest part of the work, the thing that demands the most from you either mentally or logistically?

Dealing with many of our community partners having their funding halted or stalled. The current environment where we are right now is a concern for us because we’re in a different economy right now. We keep our focus on our partners and make sure they have what they need. If they don’t [have the money they were counting on], they cannot serve as many people as they did at the same time last year.

Who do you lean on? Which other team members or partners really help you succeed?

While we work all over the City of Charlotte, our core focus is Historic West End. When we started working in that neighborhood, the first thing that we did is we reached out to J’Tanya Adams, who is the executive director for Historic West End Partners. They’re the economic and small business development arm of the community and she’s a resident as well, so we knew that we needed to partner with her for us to really dig deep on community development and engagement.

What's one mistake or failure that taught you something essential about your work?

In March of 2020, none of us knew that we would be in the middle of a pandemic. We were [working on] housing, but we weren’t sure about our next initiative. Because we were approached by the City of Charlotte to get grant dollars out to businesses, we made working with small businesses our next initiative.

We also learned that businesses needed technical assistance. There were instances where the businesses were missing paperwork or they were trying to make sure that they were getting documents to us. The transition from in-person to virtual [made that difficult], but it helped shape our small business and technical assistance programs.

How do you stay sane? What helps you keep perspective or stay grounded when the work gets overwhelming for you?

When the work starts to get hectic and I feel the load and I feel the weight, I am reminded of my upbringing. I’m reminded of my father saying “you make sure you’re taking care of yourself, but be sure you’re taking care of your community. To whom much is given, much is required.”

When things get hectic, I try to stay grounded in those words. I’m getting better at taking time off to unplug, but when I unplug, I’m still working on being my best self. It is difficult to step away because I am very passionate about this work, but I think what continues to drive me is that I feel like I have a purpose in my role: to be a leader and mentor.

What’s one essential book everyone should read?

Stop Chasing, Start Creating by Justin Jones-Fosu was recommended to me when I was opening the new office. I recommend it for folks in a similar situation, looking to get up to speed quickly.

Discover More

  • The First at 250: A Conversation on the First Amendment
  • Knight Foundation/NORC Survey on Public Libraries 2026
  • Knight Foundation/SSRS Perspectives on Free Expression Survey 2026

When LISC Charlotte looks at bringing an initiative into the city, the first thing that we do is talk to the community. One of the first things that we did was hold community meetings [across] different forums so that we could be clear on the direction community members wanted their neighborhood to take. We’ve been able to uplift projects that have been quite successful in Charlotte, simply because we were able to establish trust early on and the partners know that we have their best interests at heart.

What tools, skills or supports do you rely on to make this work happen?

None of the work or the success of LISC Charlotte would ever have happened without the LISC Charlotte team. I have an amazing staff; all of them have been with the organization since day one. They’ve been on the team for seven years and none of the work that we do [investing over $173 million in Charlotte since the office opened] would be possible without them.

What would you say is the toughest part of the work, the thing that demands the most from you either mentally or logistically?

Dealing with many of our community partners having their funding halted or stalled. The current environment where we are right now is a concern for us because we’re in a different economy right now. We keep our focus on our partners and make sure they have what they need. If they don’t [have the money they were counting on], they cannot serve as many people as they did at the same time last year.

Who do you lean on? Which other team members or partners really help you succeed?

While we work all over the City of Charlotte, our core focus is Historic West End. When we started working in that neighborhood, the first thing that we did is we reached out to J’Tanya Adams, who is the executive director for Historic West End Partners. They’re the economic and small business development arm of the community and she’s a resident as well, so we knew that we needed to partner with her for us to really dig deep on community development and engagement.

What's one mistake or failure that taught you something essential about your work?

In March of 2020, none of us knew that we would be in the middle of a pandemic. We were [working on] housing, but we weren’t sure about our next initiative. Because we were approached by the City of Charlotte to get grant dollars out to businesses, we made working with small businesses our next initiative.

We also learned that businesses needed technical assistance. There were instances where the businesses were missing paperwork or they were trying to make sure that they were getting documents to us. The transition from in-person to virtual [made that difficult], but it helped shape our small business and technical assistance programs.

How do you stay sane? What helps you keep perspective or stay grounded when the work gets overwhelming for you?

When the work starts to get hectic and I feel the load and I feel the weight, I am reminded of my upbringing. I’m reminded of my father saying “you make sure you’re taking care of yourself, but be sure you’re taking care of your community. To whom much is given, much is required.”

When things get hectic, I try to stay grounded in those words. I’m getting better at taking time off to unplug, but when I unplug, I’m still working on being my best self. It is difficult to step away because I am very passionate about this work, but I think what continues to drive me is that I feel like I have a purpose in my role: to be a leader and mentor.

What’s one essential book everyone should read?

Stop Chasing, Start Creating by Justin Jones-Fosu was recommended to me when I was opening the new office. I recommend it for folks in a similar situation, looking to get up to speed quickly.

Discover More

  • The First at 250: A Conversation on the First Amendment
  • Knight Foundation/NORC Survey on Public Libraries 2026
  • Knight Foundation/SSRS Perspectives on Free Expression Survey 2026

item.title: Meer lezen
item.description:
BRUSSELS / RIBERALTA - From Brussels to Riberalta, the ‘pearl of the Bolivian Amazon’. An investigation into the European frontier of green finance: the carbon credit market is targeting Bolivia’s indigenous territories, whose rights are at risk of being trampled on. One controversial project shows the dangers involved to frontline communities.

In the heart of the Amazon rainforest in Bolivia, home to more than 30 indigenous communities, Indigenous leaders are currently fighting to defend their territories and natural resources from European and global green policy measures, promoted as a solution to climate change. The EU has recently allowed for carbon credits to make up part of its emissions targets for 2050, accelerating already growing demand for credit, mostly generated in the Global South. In Bolivia, the EU has facilitated the opening of a new market for credits, mainly from forest protection programmes in the Amazon. But one such project, led by a Bolivian politician whose foundation planned to sell credits, was torn up after affected indigenous groups claimed they had been misled and exploited. Through this project, which indigenous leaders compared to a return to colonial land expropriation, we can see how European interest in carbon credits creates incentives for state and private actors to undermine or roll back the hard-won customary rights of frontline indigenous communities in the Amazon.

Key findings

  • Europe’s target of climate neutrality by 2050 and its role in opening up Bolivia to carbon credits.
  • The carbon credit strategy in European policy: a break for polluters.
  • The European Global Gateway strategy and the substantial funds earmarked for Bolivia, which the EU has only disclosed via FOI.
  • The carbon credit agreement that the Multiethnic Indigenous Territory II, known as TIM II, rejects: 88 per cent of the area’s 407,585 hectares is at risk of being controlled by a private foundation for 30 years.
  • In the name of carbon credits, free, prior and informed consent - indigenous of TIM II denounce - has been violated (ILO Convention No. 169).
  • Carbon credits represent a continuation of the colonial approach: a statement by Survival International.
  • From the production of Brazil nuts to carbon credits: a member of the Bolivian national parliament - of Swiss origin and with companies across Europe - proposes legislation on carbon credits whilst simultaneously investing in the sector.
  • Europe in Bolivia: the role of Team Europe (Germany, Sweden, France, Italy and Spain).
  • The false promise that violates the rights of indigenous peoples: a warning from the Solón Foundation.
  • The illusion of change to maintain the status quo: the view of the Green Finance Observatory.
  • Global polluting companies are targeting Bolivia to generate large quantities of carbon credits and continue emitting greenhouse gases: the view of the Bolivian Centre for Legal and Social Studies (CEJIS).

Methodology

The investigation was carried out by four journalists and a photojournalist: two team members in Bolivia and three in Europe. Alongside our fieldwork in the Bolivian Amazon amongst the indigenous communities affected by the carbon credit deal, we carried out research into documents, first-hand accounts, interviews, data analysis, formal requests for data via FOIA, financial investigations, the examination of reports and the analysis of company databases. We divided the areas of investigation amongst the team members, making the most of our multilingual skills and our presence in different countries, and benefited from the support of our mentor, Lionell Faull, for fact-checking, corporate research and information management.

Themes

  • Environment
  • Energy

Publication

ONLINE

  • ‘Carbon fever’ threatens hard-won Indigenous rights in Bolivian Amazon, The Guardian, 15/09/2026

COUNTRIES

  • Belgium
  • Bolivia

Team members

Ruairí Casey

Ruairí Casey is a Berlin-based journalist who specialises in housing, migration and politics

Abby Young-Powell

Abby Young-Powell is an independent British journalist based in Berlin.

Sara Aliaga Ticona

Sara Aliaga Ticona is an Aymara, journalist, visual artist, photojournalist, and filmmaker from Bolivia.

Lisa Mirella Corti

Lisa Mirella Corti is an investigative multimedia journalist.

Maria Cristina Fraddosio

Maria Cristina Fraddosio is an Italian multimedia investigative journalist.

Mentors

Lionel Faull

Lionel Faull is Investigations Editor for Lighthouse Reports, based in Autralia.

Related projects

  • © Michael Bird

    Europe, the Uranium Hell

    BUCHAREST - The EU's focus on achieving energy independence is endangering the environment and the health of its citizens due to the continued exploitation of European uranium resources.

    Meer lezen
  • © rr

    For sale: Hot air

    BUDAPEST - One year ago, the Belgian government purchased two million tonnes of CO₂ emission rights from Hungary. This €26 million investment is intended to help the country meet its obligations under the Kyoto Protocol to reduce emissions by 7.5 per cent by 2012 compared to 1990 levels.

    Meer lezen
  • © Nick Meynen

    The big carbon fraud

    MUMBAI - With financial support from the Fonds Pascal Decroos, Nick Meynen followed carbon credit money flowing from Belgium to India, where he discovered a desert full of mirages. Part from the fraud and abuse, he also noticed the difference in approach between Flanders and Belgium, the buyers of carbon credits.

    Meer lezen
